Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.50 8.2 More group actions and Cayley’s Theorem Example 8.2.1 (Important example). We are used to thinking of S5 acting on the set {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, but it can also act on the following sets: 1. X = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} with λ(g)x = {gx if 1 ≤ x ≤ 5; and x if 6 ≤ x ≤ 8 (Check that you agree this is an action, by verifying that (1) and (2) from Definition 8.1.1 both hold). 2. X = Z. For x ∈ X write x = 5n + k for some n ∈ Z and 1 ≤ k ≤ 5, and define, λ(g)x = 5n + gk. (Check that you agree this is an action, by verifying that (1) and (2) from Definition 8.1.1 both hold). 3. X = {{1, 2}, {1, 3}, {1, 4}, {1, 5}, {2, 3}, {2, 4}, {2, 5}, {3, 4}, {3, 5}, {4, 5}} (all pairs of distinct integers be- tween 1 and 5) with λ(g){a, b} = {ga, gb}. (Check that you agree this is an action, by verifying that (1) and (2) from Definition 8.1.1 both hold). Recall that an action λ is a homomorphism, and so we can talk about things like the kernel and image of the action. Proposition 8.2.2. Let λ be an action of a group G on a set X. The kernel of λ is those elements in g that fix every x ∈ X, Ker(λ) = {g ∈ G ∶ λ(g)x = x ∀x ∈ X}. Proof. Note that λ(g)x = x for all x ∈ X holds if and only if λ(g) = e. But λ(g) = e if and only if g ∈ Ker(λ). Theorem 8.2.3. (Cayley’s Theorem) Every group is isomorphic to a permutation group. Proof. Let X = G, with λ(g)x = gx for all g ∈ G and x ∈ X. We have seen this before in Example 8.1.7 (it is called the regular action) and so we know already this is an action. Let H = Im(λ) and note that H ≤ Sym(X), so H is a permutation group. Since λ is a homomorphism, we can apply the First Isomorphism Theorem to obtain that G/Ker(λ) ≅ Im(λ) = H. If we can show that Ker(λ) = ⟨e⟩, then (because G/⟨e⟩ = G) we will have proven that G ≅ H and our proof will be complete. So, suppose g ∈ Ker(λ). Then g ∈ G and gx = x for all x ∈ X. Since X = G we know that X is a group, so we have gxx−1 = xx −1. Hence g = e. Thus, Ker(λ) = ⟨e⟩. What is the point?!. We’ve already seen that every permutation group is a group. Now Cayley’s Theorem is telling us that every group can be viewed as a permutation group (called its permutation representation).
